newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Howard blamed for damaging Australia "race debacle".
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Howard blamed for damaging Australia "race debacle".

text.p: A leading aboriginal official said on Thursday that Australian Prime Minister John Howard had to bear a "large degree of responsibility" for the country's damaging race row.

In his annual report to government, aboriginal social justice commissioner Michael Dodson said Howard's push to replace 'political correctness' with 'free speech' since the March election had encouraged overt racism.
"I make no bones about the fact -- I attribute a large degree of this climatic shift to the Coalition Government and the leadership of...John Howard," Dodson wrote.

Australia has been embroiled in a national debate on race since independent politician Pauline Hanson told parliament in September that the country risked being swamped by Asians. She also complained that Aborigines were receiving unfair economic assistance from the government.
Howard, a conservative, has been criticised at home and abroad for not quickly and clearly repudiating Hanson's speech to kill off the race debate.

Conservative Howard initially defended Hanson's right to express her opinions and argued repeatedly that he did not need to respond to declarations by maverick parliamentary ministers. After ousting the "politically correct" Labor prime minister Paul Keating, Howard has pushed for Australians to be allowed a more robust debate over sensitive issues such as immigration. Dodson, appointed four years ago to monitor the human rights of indigenous Australians, said Howard's appeal for free speech had encouraged racist attitudes to surface, as had his silence over Hanson's remarks.

"It is unfortunate that because of what I perceive as a total lack of leadership on his part in relation to this debacle that's called a racism debate, that, in a sense, gives those who hold extreme views in our society the licence to be intolerant," Dodson told a news conference to launch his report.
"It's perhaps not so much his words, but it's his silence that does it."

Dodson said Howard's failure to condemn Hanson flowed from an acceptance of the core premise of her argument -- that all Australians should be treated equally, even if Aborigines or other indigenous Australians had special needs.
That acceptance meant special rights gained by Aborigines, such as native land rights, were themselves seen as racist, thus fanning prejudice and intolerance.
Elsewhere in his report, Dodson detailed the plight of Aborigines, who have markedly lower life expectancies than other Australians.

According to the latest statistics, Dodson said, aboriginal children were on average more than 20 times more likely to be locked up in corrective institutions than other children, and 41 times as likely to be so in conservative Queensland state.
"The problem is that, for some Australians, racial stereotypes and attitudes of discrimination are so deeply embedded in their psyche that they cannot even recognise them," Dodson said. "
It is clear that our neighbours and the rest of the world have a different perspective. The world will give us a reality check, if we cannot do it ourselves.
It may be an expensive check," he added.
